description:
VitalSpace is a multidisciplinary team of students from Paysandú dedicated to safeguarding the health of space explorers. We combine software and science to build a self-assessment tool that enables astronauts to track their health metrics, interpret them, and take timely action when help is far away. We believe that going further requires taking care of those who make it possible.

Our logo represents the constellation Ophiuchus, associated with Asclepius, the god of medicine.
summary:
VitalSpace is a web-based health self-check tool for astronauts on long-duration missions, where Earth-based medical support is delayed or unavailable. Each astronaut completes one daily check-up (resting heart rate, blood pressure, fasting glucose, temperature, sleep, mood, exercise and radiation dose). The app colour-codes an interactive body map from Stable to Severe, draws trend charts, records symptoms by body area, and raises alerts that explain the problem and recommended action, based on reference ranges and each astronaut’s baseline. Points and motivational messages encourage consistent monitoring and support mental well-being. Its content is grounded in NASA’s OCHMO medical standards, radiation technical brief, and Human Research Program risk reports. It addresses the challenge by letting crews detect health changes in themselves and act on them autonomously. It matters because small changes caught early can prevent serious events when evacuation is impossible. Built with HTML, CSS, JavaScript, PHP and MariaDB, it can grow by connecting to wearables and medical devices so data fills in automatically. Finally, the project is hosted at https://vitalspace.duckdns.org/ using a free Dynamic DNS (DDNS) service called DuckDNS, which allows access to the website from a server belonging to one of the team members.
* The server will only be available for a limited time during the event.
details:
VitalSpace is a web app for astronaut self-monitoring during long-duration missions. The astronaut chooses an account and completes one check-up per day (the database rejects a second one for the same date). The check-up records eight indicators: resting heart rate, systolic blood pressure, fasting glucose, body temperature, sleep, mood, exercise minutes and radiation dose.

Each value is compared with a reference range and given a status: Stable, Mild, Moderate or Severe. An interactive body map (head, torso, abdomen, arms, legs) is coloured by the worst status among the indicators and symptoms linked to each area over the last three days. Selecting an area opens a short symptom questionnaire, saved as clinical observations with a severity level. Trend charts show each indicator against its stable band and the astronaut’s personal baseline.

Alerts state the problem and the recommended action. They are triggered by out-of-range values and by deviation from the astronaut’s own baseline (the average of their first three check-ups). An in-app reminder appears when the day’s check-up is missing. The Checkup page also lists the in-flight exams from NASA Medical Standard OCHMO-STD-100.1A (body mass measurement, jugular vein ultrasound) for the astronaut to tick off. Explanatory panels cover spaceflight stressors such as radiation, bone loss, immune changes, sleep and exercise.

What benefits does it have?

* One accessible place to track health, see changes over time and spot problems before they worsen.

* It supports autonomy: the astronaut understands each value, why it matters in space and what to do about it.

* Personal baselines make alerts relevant to the individual, not only to population ranges.

* Points, streaks and motivational messages encourage the daily routine and support mental well-being.

* Content that adapts by sex (for example, radiation-risk information) reflects NASA’s own findings.

What is the intended impact of the project?

To improve the safety, well-being and autonomy of crews on missions where immediate medical help is not available. In the long term, VitalSpace can serve as a base for more complete and adaptable self-care systems, for future space missions and for other remote or isolated environments with similar health-monitoring challenges.

What tools, coding languages, hardware or software did we use?

* HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript on the front end (SVG body map and charts, no chart libraries).

* SweetAlert2 for pop-ups; Google Fonts (Orbitron, Open Sans).

* PHP (JSON API with sessions and input validation) and MariaDB (astronauts, check-ups, observations and exam records).

* Database migration and reset scripts.

* Free Dynamic DNS (DDNS) service called 'DuckDNS' for hosting.

* Canva for the design prototype.

* No special hardware: it runs in any modern browser.

* Images: all images in the project (the VitalSpace logo and wordmark, the login background and the other interface graphics) were created by our team. No AI image generation was used.

* AI tools: Claude was used as an assistant, with human input and human-validated output; for the chart code, the simulated demo data, code comments, and code review. Also, translation, spell-check, and English drafting.

How is our project creative?

VitalSpace combines health monitoring, a visual body map, symptom tracking, personalised alerts and educational explanations in a single platform designed for space missions. Instead of showing a table of numbers, it turns NASA’s published standards and risks into clear, practical guidance the astronaut can act on, and it adds light gamification to keep the daily routine going.

Beyond its current capabilities, the project envisions integration with different medical devices and monitoring equipment, such as smartwatches, scanners and measuring instruments. This would enable automatic data collection, reducing manual input, simplifying daily check-ups and making health monitoring more efficient and convenient for astronauts.

What factors did our team consider?

* The conditions of long missions: microgravity, radiation, isolation, confinement, sleep disruption, cardiovascular change, bone loss and immune dysregulation.

* Autonomy: astronauts must be able to take measurements, interpret them and act without constant outside help.

* A clear, easy-to-use interface, good data visualisation and user motivation.

* A scientific basis in NASA documents (OCHMO-STD-100.1A, OCHMO-TB-020, NTRS reports, Human Research Program).

* Current limitations: the reference ranges are general adult references and team judgment, not NASA standards, and must be validated by a flight surgeon before real use. Login is currently passwordless (demo mode), and the video library is still being filled.

Future development

The software can be developed much further by connecting it to monitoring devices and equipment, so that measurements fill in automatically. Other planned features: daily data transmission to Earth, a missed-check-up protocol that notifies ground physicians, an emergency section for reporting a crew member’s problem, and comparison with NASA life-sciences reference data.
